title: Onprem Airgapped - artifact delivery, offline licensing & GPU drivers deep dive

Covered delivery vectors (signed tarball / encrypted USB), offline license key formats, installation checklist, and runtime concerns: CUDA/CUDNN compatibility, quantization libs, KV cache behavior, and batching windows. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share signed artifact manifest, offline license package + install guide, and benchmark script; customer to provide hardware inventory and access for pilot tests.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Northwind Infra), Daniel Ortiz (Northwind ML), Lena Fischer (Northwind Security), Tom Wu (Northwind Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Short deep-dive on artifact delivery and offline licensing for air-gapped deployment; lots of low-level driver/version and install checklist items; discussed kv cache behaviour and batching windows for latency SLOs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. We're here to run through the on-prem air-gapped delivery flow, offline license, and driver compatibility. Marcus and Sofia from our SE team will cover the runtime implications — batching, kv cache, quantization — and I'll handle the packaging and licensing bits.

[00:18] Priya (Northwind): Thanks, Alex. Quick context: we're setting up a COLO in FRA region, fully air-gapped, no outbound internet from the inference cluster. Target is 200 qps steady state for our summarization model, p95 latency under 180ms if possible. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated on-prem package.

[00:35] Marcus (Redwood SE): Cool. Quick clarifying q: when you say 200 qps, is that single model variant or mix? Also sequence length distribution?

[00:44] Daniel (Northwind): Mostly single variant, prod prompts avg 256 tokens, peaks at 512. Mix is 85% short, 15% long.

[00:52] Marcus: Got it. That distribution actually favors keeping the KV cache warm most of the time which helps. We'll talk about batching window and continuous batching to keep latency tight.

[01:05] Lena (Security): From security side we need: signed artifact manifests, attestation of binaries, and an offline activation flow that doesn't require outbound callbacks. Also SOC2 doc and list of what telemetry (if any) is emitted during runtime.

[01:18] Alex: Absolutely. Our offline license is a signed token bundle — we provide a PKI-signed license file and an activation script you run locally. No callbacks required; activation is local. We'll include a SHA256 manifest and GPG signatures for each artifact.

[01:32] Tom (Procurement): For procurement we need to know if the GPU drivers are included or if we need to license separately from the hardware vendor. Also any third-party binary redistributions?

[01:44] Sofia (Redwood): Good question. We ship our runtime artifacts and the optimized operator libs. GPU drivers — typically NVIDIA — are provided as vendor packages. For air-gapped installs we can provide the exact driver versions and offline installer tarballs, but licensing for the drivers stays with the vendor. We will include the checksums and an install checklist.

[01:58] Priya: So you provide the driver tarball? And we handle license with NVIDIA?

[02:05] Sofia: We can provide the tarball/installer we tested against — e.g., NVIDIA driver r515 or r530 depending on CUDA matrix — but if there's a commercial driver license requirement you handle that via your vendor contract. We also provide a compatibility matrix.

[02:18] Daniel: What's the recommended CUDA/CUDNN combo for your quantized runtime? We want int8 perf where possible.

[02:26] Marcus: For our quantization-friendly path we recommend CUDA 12.2 + cuDNN 9.x for best kernel selection, and we test extensively against those. For some NVidia card families older CUDA like 11.8 is supported, but performance and kernel availability for fused attention and int8 can vary. We'll include notes in the matrix.

[02:44] Priya: Any special kernel modules or ktune we need to preinstall?

[02:49] Marcus: No special ktune. The usual driver + container runtime (we support containerd and docker) and we have a thin runtime shim. For air-gapped we provide container images as tarballs and a deployment manifest for your orchestrator.

[03:05] Priya: Great. On the offline license: can you walk through the activation steps?

[03:10] Alex: Sure. We give you: 1) signed license file — license.json.sig, 2) activation utility (binary) with its checksum, 3) a one-line command you run on the control plane node that consumes the license file and writes the local license to /etc/redwood/license, and 4) an offline-proof file you optionally send back via secure transfer for audit. None of these require outbound calls.

[03:30] Lena: I want to confirm we can do key rotation and that we get an audit log of license installs.

[03:35] Alex: We log license activation locally and produce a signed install artifact; we can surface the activation event in the admin console if you choose to run the control plane connected, but for air-gapped we provide the log file and optional signed attestations. Key rotation for activation keys is supported — we'll outline the process.

[03:50] Tom: On procurement, what about driver offline licensing — do you provide guidance on which vendor SKUs to buy?

[03:56] Sofia: We'll include recommended SKUs per card family and a recommended node layout for the throughput target. For 200 qps with average seq 256 we usually recommend N GPUs of type A100 40GB (example), but we'll provide a range and expected throughput per card from our benchmarks.

[04:20] Daniel: Can you share an example of your benchmark numbers for a similar workload? Even ballpark p95 and throughput per GPU.

[04:28] Marcus: Yes. For a 256-token avg seq with quantized int8 model on A100 we typically see ~120-150 qps per GPU with p95 around 80-140 ms depending on batching window and KV cache hit rate. Those numbers change with quantization profile and attention kernel selection. We'll share the raw benchmark scripts.

[04:50] Priya: You mentioned KV cache hit rates — what's the expected behavior on warm vs cold starts?

[04:57] Marcus: Cold start you'll pay for the full autoregressive pass until the KV cache warms. With steady-state similar prompts you'll see high KV reuse and much higher effective throughput. We recommend a warmup ramp phase for pilots to prefill caches. Our benchmark script includes a warmup phase.

[05:15] Priya: Okay. How much disk / RAM is used by KV cache for our model size?

[05:20] Marcus: For your model (70B quantized) expect roughly X GB per KV per sequence length; I'll be precise in the doc but ballpark: ~0.5-1.2 GB per 512 tokens per beam depending on kv storage format and quantization. We'll provide exact numbers in the inventory doc.

[05:40] Daniel: There's a transcription artefact here — I think it said 'X GB' — can we get concrete numbers?

[05:45] Marcus: Yes — apologies, that's my verbal placeholder. Concrete: for our 70B quantized footprint with 512 token max, KV cache approx 0.9 GB per request stream; we'll put a table.

[05:58] Priya: Installer packaging — what are the delivery options? We prefer an encrypted USB for FedRAMP-ish process, but can accept SFTP with air-gapped handshake.

[06:08] Alex: We support both. Options: 1) Signed tarball + manifest via SFTP server you host (we can push), 2) Encrypted USB with hardware crypto and tamper-evident packaging (courier), or 3) Signed container images as OCI tarballs handed over via secure transfer. For each option we provide SHA256 and GPG signatures. For FedRAMP we often recommend couriered encrypted media.

[06:30] Tom: Cost implication? Is there a fee for couriered delivery or offline license?

[06:34] Alex: Usually courier costs are passed through; offline license packaging is part of the enterprise plan but we can put specifics in the contract annex.

[06:45] Lena: About telemetry: we need explicit list of any outbound network calls if the control plane is connected later, and a privacy sheet for what the runtime logs.

[06:55] Alex: We'll give a telemetry matrix. For air-gapped, by default telemetry is disabled; logs are local. If you opt-in for support telemetry later, we use encrypted egress over TLS and you control what is shared. We'll document log schemas.

[07:10] Daniel: Back to runtime: batching windows — how do you recommend tuning to hit 180ms p95 while keeping cost low?

[07:18] Marcus: It's a tradeoff. Short batching windows (2-5ms) favor latency but lower throughput. For 200 qps with avg seq 256, we typically open a batching window of ~8-12ms combined with continuous batching and prefix caching to hit p95 targets while keeping GPU utilization high. We'll include a chart in the docs.

[07:35] Priya: Do you support adaptive batching?

[07:38] Marcus: Yes, we have adaptive batching that expands or shrinks based on current latency SLO and queue depth. It also respects per-route max latency.

[07:45] Daniel: How about model fallback if a GPU is down or drivers don't match? Automated fallback to CPU or smaller model?

[07:52] Sofia: We have policy-based routing — can fallback to a smaller quantized variant or CPU pool, but for air-gapped you need to have those variants available locally. We'll describe the fallback plan and how to store model variants in the artifact bundle.

[08:06] Priya: For the artifact bundle, how big are the model artifacts and how do you recommend transfer?

[08:12] Alex: The quantized 70B model bundle is usually ~40-60GB depending on quantization and sharding. For air-gapped we suggest shipping on encrypted SSDs or shipping compressed OCI layers as tarballs. We'll include exact sizes per variant.

[08:28] Tom: What's the checksum/verification step? We need instructions to verify integrity upon receipt.

[08:33] Alex: We'll deliver a SHA256 manifest and a GPG-signed manifest file. Steps: verify signature, compute checksum of tarball, decompress and verify internal checksums. We'll include verification script.

[08:46] Lena: Any guidance on offline OS patch management? We need to know kernel modules compatibility beyond drivers.

[08:52] Marcus: We'll include an OS compatibility matrix; kernel versions matter for certain driver stacks. Recommend matching our tested Linux distro (we'll supply exact distro snapshot) or use a certified distro image we provide.

[09:05] Daniel: A quick question on quantization: can you support per-layer mixed precision? We've seen regressions with aggressive int8 on some attention layers.

[09:12] Marcus: Yes, we support mixed quantization profiles. We have a conservative default to preserve quality and an aggressive profile to maximize throughput. During the pilot bench we recommend running quality evals on your prompt set to ensure no regression; we can help run those locally.

[09:30] Priya: If we want to run the pilot, what access do you need? SSH to a bastion or just the offline node with the artifacts?

[09:36] Sofia: For initial pilot, we usually ask for: 1) hardware inventory + IPs for orchestration planning, 2) a bastion access with controlled jump hosts for remote SE assistance during the run, or 3) schedule an on-site SE visit. If you are strictly no remote access, we will walk through the install and you run the benchmarks and share logs.

[09:55] Priya: Prefer bastion with restricted access; we'll provide jumpbox credentials for the pilot window.

[10:02] Tom: For procurement: can you provide a packing list for what we should order from our hardware vendor so we can raise the PO?

[10:08] Alex: Yes, we'll provide an appendix with recommended SKUs, node layout, expected performance per GPU, and a rough BOM for rack-level planning.

[10:20] Daniel: One last thing — offline license expiry/renewal. How is that handled for renewals in air-gapped mode?

[10:26] Alex: We produce license files with expiry metadata. Renewals are done by issuing a new signed license bundle which you apply the same way via the activation utility. We can also script rolling renewals for large fleets.

[10:40] Lena: Do you support HSM integration for license keys if we want to lock keys to a TPM?

[10:46] Marcus: We have optional HSM/TPM hooks; license activation can be bound to a machine id or hardware TPM endorsement. We'll include the integration notes; for air-gapped customers we sometimes do TPM binding for extra security.

[10:58] Priya: That sounds good. Can you also include the list of file paths and services we need to open on the internal network if we decide to connect the control plane later?

[11:06] Alex: Yes, we'll include a network port matrix and an explicit list of egress requirements (if any). For fully air-gapped, none are required.

[11:18] Daniel: Let's talk about edge cases — what if the driver we tested fails on your hardware revision?

[11:24] Sofia: In that case we have a runbook: collect logs, fallback to smaller quantized model or CPU, and we can ship an updated operator patch. We also support on-site debugging planes. For urgent issues we can provide hotfix tarballs.

[11:40] Priya: Ok let's finalize next steps.

[11:43] Alex: Recap — Redwood will: 1) share signed artifact bundle (model variants + runtime + container images) with SHA256 and GPG signatures, 2) provide the offline license package and activation script, 3) share GPU driver tarballs we've validated plus compatibility matrix, 4) benchmark script and warmup sequence, and 5) procurement appendix. Customer will: provide hardware inventory, decide on transfer method (encrypted USB vs SFTP), and schedule pilot window.

[12:10] Priya: Sounds good. Any blockers from your side?

[12:13] Alex: No blockers. We'll aim to get the signed artifact manifest to you within 48 hours.

[12:20] Tom: Procurement will review the appendix and come back with PO questions.

[12:24] Lena: Security will review the license activation walkthrough and telemetry matrix.

[12:28] Daniel: We'll coordinate pilot dates after we send the hardware inventory.

[12:33] Alex: Great. We'll send the secure transfer link and schedule the pilot slot once we have inventory. Thanks everyone.

[12:40] (Call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions and placeholders present; speaker labels simplified where auto-generated.
